titleEn: In the LORD I take refuge
progression: | Em Em | Am Em | C D | Em Em |
intro: Seven verses that work as an argument. Someone tells David to run for the hills, and he refuses the advice in the opening line before spending the rest of the psalm explaining why. It falls on the second day of the monthly cycle, where the reading runs from Psalm 10 to Psalm 17. The grammar to watch is a pair of roots that cross the two halves: the verb for beholding appears at {{4.7}} and again at {{7.6}}, the verb for testing at {{4.9}} and again at {{5.2}}. What God does to people in the middle of the psalm is what the upright get to do at the end.

stichs.en: For the choirmaster. Of David.
In the LORD I have taken refuge.
How can you say to me: flee to your mountain, bird!

verses.summary: The psalm opens on a refusal. The advice to run is quoted only so it can be dismissed, and the Hebrew leaves the bird without any word of comparison, which is why translations disagree about who is being called one. Note also that the imperative at word 7 is feminine singular, addressed to the soul, while the possessive on the mountain is plural.

stichs.en: For look, the wicked bend a bow,
they have set their arrow on the string,
to shoot from the dark at the upright of heart.

verses.summary: The reason for the panic: an ambush that is already prepared. The stages come in order, bending, fitting, aiming, and the target is named last. Nothing in the psalm ever says the bow was unbent.

stichs.en: When the foundations are torn down,
what has the righteous one achieved?

verses.summary: The advice ends in a question with no answer built into it. Depending on how the first word is taken, this is either the counsellor's despair or David's summary of what the counsellor means.

stichs.en: The LORD is in His holy palace,
the LORD, His throne is in the heavens.
His eyes behold,
His eyelids test humankind.

verses.summary: The answer starts with a location rather than an argument. Two clauses fix God in a palace and on a throne, and only then does the psalm mention eyes, so the seeing comes from somewhere settled rather than from nowhere in particular.

stichs.en: The LORD tests the righteous one,
but the wicked and the lover of violence His soul hates.

verses.summary: Testing replaces fleeing as the account of what a hard life is. The verb that stood in the plural in the previous verse comes back here in the singular with God as its subject, which ties the two verses into one statement.

stichs.en: He will rain snares upon the wicked;
fire and brimstone and a scorching wind,
the portion of their cup.

verses.summary: The one verse of retribution, and it is entirely weather. The nouns arrive faster than the syntax can hold them, which is part of why the first of them is disputed.

stichs.en: For the LORD is righteous,
He loves righteous acts;
the upright will behold His face.

verses.summary: The close answers the opening. Refuge was claimed in verse 1 with no reason attached; the reason given here is God's own character, and what the upright are promised is not safety but sight.

pardes.body: The psalm is a reply, and the thing being replied to is quoted first. Verses 1 to 3 belong to the advisers: flee, the ambush is set, the foundations are going. Verses 4 to 7 are the answer, and the answer denies none of it. The bow stays bent. What changes is the vantage point, from ground level where arrows come out of the dark to a throne from which the dark is not dark. No rescue is promised anywhere in the text. What is promised is that the looking runs in both directions.

Two words carry most of the difficulty. At {{6.3}} the noun means traps or snares everywhere else it appears, yet it sits at the head of a list of fire words, so translations split between snares and burning coals; the JPS line printed above chose coals. At {{7.7}} the ending is an archaic poetic suffix, and it has been read both as His face, the thing the upright get to see, and as their faces, which would make the upright the ones being seen. The same verse also puts a singular subject at {{7.5}} in front of a plural verb, a mismatch Hebrew tolerates when the singular names a type rather than a person.

Verse 3 is the line that gets quoted on its own, usually as a question about what a decent person can still do once the structures are down. Inside the psalm it is not an open question at all: it is the last thing the advisers say before being answered, and the answer is verse 4. The fire and brimstone of verse 6 point back to Sodom in Genesis 19, which is the Bible's standing case of a place whose foundations were destroyed, and the place where the question of what the righteous accomplish had already been put to God out loud by Abraham.

The two beholding verbs frame the psalm as one act of vision with two directions. God's eyes and eyelids test in verse 4, the upright behold in verse 7, and a single verb serves both, so being examined and being able to look are described as one event rather than two. The eyelid is the odd term. An eye that narrows is an eye adjusting to what it is looking at, and the image gives the divine gaze a measure, a squint, instead of a flat and effortless omniscience.
